Claude Code plugin marketplace · autonomous coding

One engineer, asleep.
Several features, shipping.

Run a coding agent unattended overnight — packaged as plugins, gated where it counts, and built around the one hard problem: knowing when the work is actually done.

You launch one command before bed. By morning, a queue of features has been built in parallel, verified end-to-end, and the safe ones have merged themselves to a green main — while anything risky or ambiguous waits, clearly, for you.

📦 5 plugins, installed not copied 🧪 28 suites · 493+ assertions, built test-first 🧑‍⚖️ human-gated where it counts 💳 subscription-friendly (no API key required)
The load-bearing idea: an agent must never be the judge of its own completion. "Done" is an external, machine-checkable contract — get that wrong and the run either quits early or never stops. Everything here serves that one truth.

Same machinery, different gate

Both flavors share every subsystem — planner, DoD verify, worktree builds, serial merge queue, guards, digest (the loop, the DoD). The only difference: the gated flavor keeps the per-PR human OK before anything reaches main; run-to-completion replaces it with the risk gate — and only for low-risk epics.

Mental model

Three laws to design against

The model is the engine; the harness is everything around it that makes an unattended run safe, verifiable, and resumable.

🧠The repo is the only memory

Each session starts amnesiac — like shift workers who never met. Anything not in the repo, git history, or the state layer does not exist next session. Externalize state; never rely on the conversation.

🔍Verification is the bottleneck

Generation is cheap; trustworthy verification is not. The whole game is moving "is this correct?" off the human and into mechanical loops — tests, browser checks, linters, adversarial reviewers.

🧑‍✈️Humans steer, agents execute

You design the environment, specify intent, and own the gates that carry product and security judgment. The machine does the volume between those gates.

🔧A failure is a harness bug

When the agent fails, the question is never "try harder" — it's "what capability or signal was missing, and how do I make it legible and enforceable?"

What it must defeat

The four ways an overnight run rots

01

One-shotting

Tries to do everything at once, exhausts its context mid-feature, leaves a half-built mess. Parry: one unit of work per session; a locked scope.

02

Premature victory (project)

A late session sees progress and declares the whole project finished. Parry: a feature list that defines finished — done when every item passes, not before.

03

Premature victory (feature)

Marks a feature done after a unit test or a curl, never exercising it as a user would. Parry: end-to-end browser verification, defined up front.

04

Dirty state

Leaves bugs and disordered code the next shift inherits at interest. Parry: "clean state" = mergeable; commit + progress note every session.

Getting started

Install the plugins

It ships as a plugin marketplace, not a copied repo: one versioned dependency many projects share and upgrade in place. Installing a plugin is the on/off switch; skills are namespaced (/orchestrator:run, /orchestrator:kickoff, …).

# add once, install the core, then reload so its skills register
/plugin marketplace add lbtbly/agentic-harness-template-plugin
/plugin install core@harness
/reload-plugins

# stand up a project, then add the autonomous loop
/core:new-project
/plugin install orchestrator@harness   &&   /reload-plugins
/orchestrator:enable-orchestrator
The reload gotcha

A freshly installed plugin's skills are "Unknown command" until you run /reload-plugins. It's baked into every install instruction here — the single most common "why doesn't the command exist" stumble.

Two prompts, one harness

/core:new-project is the initializer — it builds the environment once (feature-list scaffolds, a one-command app launch, the first commit). Every session afterward is the same coder prompt: incremental progress, one unit, clean exit.

UI projects: the design pair

Answer web UI to the scaffolder's UI-surface question and it deep-merges settings-design.json into the project's .claude/settings.json: two third-party plugins — impeccable (anti-slop detector hooks after every UI edit + a Stop deep pass, plus /impeccable audit·critique·polish…) and styles-library (style-picker direction briefs) — declared with autoUpdate: true, so Claude Code offers the install on repo trust and refreshes them in the background. The workflow it prints: pick the direction with style-picker, capture it via /impeccable init into DESIGN.md, and the hooks enforce it from then on (Node ≥ 22 required for the hooks; ADR-0031).

Turning autonomy on — the six preconditions

/orchestrator:enable-orchestrator verifies, doesn't trust: if any precondition is missing it stops and lists what's absent. Two of the six bend where the environment cannot supply them — by recorded decision, never by drift (rows 4 and 5).

#PreconditionWhy
1autonomous profilechosen at scaffold (or confirm the upgrade)
2A green test suitethe loop verifies against your tests — new-project ships a green day-0 suite (smoke test + runner), so this has a target from the start
3Staging deploy command + URLeach night's integration branch deploys so you (and it) can exercise it
4Sandbox devcontainerdefault-deny egress firewall — unattended execution stays boxed in. The local runtime may substitute a fail-closed OS sandbox on your own machine (ADR-0033)
5Branch protection on mainverified via the forge API; the agent's token cannot bypass it — deny-rules alone can't stop a refspec push. Where the forge can't provide it (private repo, free GitHub plan: no protection, no rulesets), accept it once via forgeProtection: "unavailable-accepted" — which force-disables auto-merge, so every merge stays human (ADR-0032)
6A forge (github/gitlab)every operator signal (plan approval, per-PR OK/revise) is read from the forge, never the board
Reversible

/orchestrator:disable-orchestrator removes the loop (schedule, risk policy, run profile) but preserves the board and all its data, past digests, and committed settings. The board outlives the orchestrator; enable and disable freely.

How it runs

Two flavors, and a typical day

gated Scheduled nightly — the recommended default

A scheduled build produces one PR per epic overnight; each morning you review and merge. Every human gate stays — plans approved by you, nothing reaches main without your per-PR OK.

auto Run-to-completion

/orchestrator:run — point it at an initiative or the whole board and it drains the scope. Landing needs low risk AND a class that has earned tier auto; everything else escalates. Keeps the plan gate, trades the per-PR merge gate for a risk-plus-trust gate. A fresh install has no ledger, so the first nights produce reviewed PRs whichever flavor you pick — autonomy arrives per corner of the codebase, as evidence accumulates.

A day in the gated flavor — one morning touchpoint

~09:00

you Review last night's PRs

The digest arrives — your worklist. Per PR: test it on staging following the ordered sequence, then leave one signal: /orch approve or /orch revise: <notes>. Give the high-risk flags the closer read.

~11:00

you · ~15 min Run /orchestrator:kickoff

Reads your OK/revise signals from the forge (matched via the orch/<id> branch), risk-checks then merges OK'd + green PRs one-by-one (full suite after each; a red merge is reverted), queues commented PRs for rework (missing-context notes become proposed rules you approve), drafts plans for new epics — you approve each plan live (the plan gate) — then partitions files and detaches.

~12:30 →

the machine The build runs itself

Fires on the schedule inside the egress-locked sandbox under its own permission profile: one worker per epic in its own worktree — reworks the commented ones, builds the new ones, independently verifies each epic against its DoD before integrating (not the builder's own word for it), integrates serially, checks overlaps, waits for CI and repairs what it can, deploys staging, writes tomorrow's digest. A usage limit pauses it; it resumes on reset.

The loop

Run-to-completion, as a pipeline

The driver owns an outer loop. Steps 1–2 need you briefly at launch; 3–7 run unattended until your selected scope is drained or a guard trips. Every round re-reads the board, so a killed run resumes without rebuilding settled work.

01

Launch & scope

An initiative, all epics in order, or the first N — it lists their names to confirm, and folds in the previous run's PR feedback. Scope comes from the board, which is the golden source.

gated by run/SKILL.md run-to-done.sh · select_scope()
02

Blindspot pass, then plan

Unknown unknowns are named first — what is unfamiliar, what has been tried, what "good" looks like here — and the questions whose answers would change the architecture get asked before anything is authored. A DoD written at 6pm on a wrong assumption wastes the whole night. Then: oversized initiatives decompose into right-sized epics with real deps[]; any epic without a DoD gets one; an independent reviewer validates each DoD against intent before a line is built.

gated by plan/SKILL.md planner.md design-reviewer.md validate-dod
03

Admit a wave, then build

Admission is three filters in order: dependency-topological on deps[] (an epic waits until every dep has landed), then footprint-disjoint so no two epics write the same files, then capped by the usage throttle. The wave is built once, one subagent per epic in its own worktree. A dependency cycle stops the run with DEPS.

gated by nightly-orchestrator.js · Build phase run-to-done.sh · partition_wave()
04

Verify — the DoD

Each epic loops build → verify → improve until the independent four-stage DoD passes. A no-progress guard breaks stubborn epics out to escalation. Both flavors verify independently — the nightly used to integrate on the builder's own self-report; it now runs dod-verify before integrating too.

gated by dod-verify.js dod-verdict.js feature-list.schema.json
05

Integrate, then land — serially

A single merge queue: integrate → cross-epic regression → risk classify → trust check. Landing needs low risk AND tier auto; anything else escalates. The local merge is the run-local integration proof — clean merge plus a green suite, serial, so each epic is verified against everything landed before it. The landing is then requested through the forge with --auto, leaving branch protection and CODEOWNERS as the enforcer. The driver never pushes main.

gated by run-to-done.sh · merge_epic() / compute_risk() risk-policy.json integration-checker.md
06

Guard & throttle

Budget, wall-clock, no-progress, thrash and safety guards bound the run; the usage monitor halves the concurrency cap at 80% and pauses at 95%, then the retry lane resumes on reset. Stop reasons are explicit: DEPS (cycle), USAGE (paused), THRASH (a whole wave returned no usable verdict — the engine is failing, not the code), BUDGET, WALLCLOCK, SAFETY. A budget cap with no spend signal says so loudly rather than pretending to be guarded.

gated by run-to-done.sh · guard_*() / throttle run-with-limits.sh
07

Terminate

Ends when every selected epic is merged, escalated or blocked — or a hard guard trips with a clean checkpoint. It never declares the product done; only "the scope you picked is resolved." Merged epics then graduate into standing goals that keep being re-verified daily, so "done" stops being a claim about one evening.

gated by run-to-done.sh · run_loop() test-run-to-done.sh (proves it)
The crux

The definition of done

If "done" is only "the tests pass," the agent ships things that pass but are wrong. A trustworthy DoD spans engineering, product, and design — and is checked by something other than the thing that built it. That is now true of both flavors: the nightly used to integrate on the builder's own self-reported done while independent verification ran only in run-to-completion.

// per-epic .orch/epics/<id>/feature_list.json — the termination authority
{
  "epic": "checkout-v2",
  "acceptanceCriteria": [{ "id":"ac1", "statement":"user can pay with a saved card", "automated":true }],
  "testLevels": { "unit":true, "integration":true, "e2e":true },
  "epicTests": ["tests/checkout/pay.e2e.ts"],
  "designRefs": ["docs/design/checkout.png"],
  "features": [{
    "id":"f1", "description":"pay with saved card",
    "steps":["open /checkout","choose saved card","confirm"],
    "expected":"order confirmed, receipt shown", "passes": false
  }]
}

JSON, not Markdown — models corrupt structured files far less. The only permitted mutation is flipping passes to true after a real pass — and the flip must carry evidence (a screenshot path or output ref, recorded by the verifier, not the builder; a pass without proof is flagged). Editing or deleting steps to look complete is prohibited by contract and enforced by validate-dod.

1️⃣Tests, every level

Unit + integration + e2e, plus the tests authored for this epic; typecheck + lint clean. Never weaken a test to pass — fix the code.

2️⃣Functional E2E, as a user

Drive the running app in a real browser (Playwright / browser MCP), walking each feature's steps. Invisible surfaces go to blindspots, never silently passed.

3️⃣Acceptance assertions

Each product-level criterion checked — automated where possible, judge-evaluated otherwise.

4️⃣Independent judge panel

Adversarial reviewers with distinct lenses (correctness / pm / design) — and distinct models per lens, because same-model votes correlate. Pass = strict majority AND no blocking objection; dissent escalates.

// what verifyDoD(epic) returns — the merge queue's input
{ "epic":"checkout-v2", "done": false, "escalate": true,
  "stages": { "tests":"pass", "e2e":"pass", "acceptance":"pass", "judge":"fail" },
  "blocking": ["judge:correctness"], "reasons": ["saved-card path 500s on expired token"] }
No self-grading

The chain is separate at every link: the planner authors the DoD → an independent design-reviewer validates it against intent → the builder implements → an independent judge panel verifies → the forge (checks + CODEOWNERS) gates the merge. Human intent — the initiative you launched — is the root ground truth.

Honest limit

The judge panel is the load-bearing weak link — an LLM judging an LLM. Mitigations: diverse lenses and models, majority + blocking-dissent, landing only for low-risk work in a class that has earned it, and a morning report a human skims. Vision misses things (native modals, subtle regressions) — design-heavy work is flagged for human eyes. This is why auto-merge is scoped, not universal.

the contract & its enforcers feature-list.schema.json feature-list.example.json validate-dod dod-verify.js dod-verdict.js test-dod-contract.sh test-dod-verify.sh
Throughput

Parallel build, serial merge

Build wide, land narrow. Many epics build at once in isolated worktrees; a single serial queue lands them so concurrency can never race main into a broken state.

🌳Isolation

One git worktree per epic (orch/<id>); parallel builders physically cannot touch each other's files.

🌊Waves

The planner's footprint per epic partitions work: disjoint footprints run together; heavy overlaps go to a later wave to cut rework.

🚧The merge barrier

Done epics queue: integrate → cross-epic regression on overlaps → risk-gate → merge or escalate → re-run the suite on main, auto-revert on red → recreate the integration branch.

🔁Resumability

Git + the forge are the source of truth. A killed or paused run re-reads reality and continues; orphaned epics re-queue. Pause/resume and crashes are safe.

implemented in run-to-done.sh · partition_wave() + run_loop() nightly-orchestrator.js · Integrate (serial for-loop) integration-checker.md
Bounds

Guards & usage throttling

The agent is never the authority on when to stop globally — external guards are. Defer (pause and resume) ≠ halt (checkpoint and end) ≠ skip (drop one epic, keep going).

GuardScopeEffect
No-progressper epicK improve rounds with no movement → mark blocked, escalate, move on
Usage throttlerunnear the ceiling → drop concurrency → pause → auto-resume on reset (defers)
Budgetrunhard token/cost cap → checkpoint + halt
Wall-clockrun"until 07:00" / max duration → checkpoint + halt
Thrashruna whole wave returns no usable verdict — the engine is failing, not the code → halt
Depsrunwork remains but nothing is admissible: a dependency cycle, or a dep that escalated instead of landing → halt
Safetyrunsettings tampered / branch protection gone / sandbox down → abort
A guard that cannot measure says so

The budget guard needs a spend signal. Without one it reports unknown and the run prints a warning rather than reporting itself as guarded — a cap that silently never trips is worse than no cap, because you stop watching.

Throttle, don't crash

Rate limits (429s) ride the CLI's own backoff. Hard limits (a weekly/daily cap) never sleep in-process for hours — pending epics checkpoint as Paused with paused-until <ts> and their origin state, the run exits cleanly, and a retry lane resumes after the reset. The loop also picks its own weight class per epic — a cheaper model for mechanical work, a stronger one for large/risky footprints, escalating once on a hard failure.

the guards live in run-to-done.sh · guard_*() / usage_pct() / throttled_cap() run-with-limits.sh · pause/resume by class nightly-orchestrator.js · BLOCK_AFTER_ATTEMPTS / capRemaining() test-run-with-limits.sh
Organisation

The board & the epic lifecycle

Work is organised as initiatives (big asks) the planner decomposes into epics (right-sized units, each with its own DoD), holding features (one user-verifiable behaviour each). Lay a board out as these columns and it's a live picture of the loop.

The board is the golden source

Initiatives, epics and tasks live on your board — that is what "exists". .orch/ is a working mirror the agents read while work is in flight, reconciled back to the board, which always wins. A card a human wrote is picked up like any other; the harness does not have to have invented it. Cards are claimed with an expiring lease, so two agents never take the same work and a crashed agent's card returns to the pool instead of being stranded.

Suggested

Machine-proposed findings await your triage. The night loop never touches this lane.

🤖 proposes · 🧑 triage
Backlog

Initiatives you've filed or accepted, not yet planned.

🧑 you file
Needs-plan

Awaiting a plan + your approval at the next kickoff.

🧑 you / kickoff
Planned

Plan approved by you — cleared to build.

🧑 plan gate
In-progress

A worker is building or reworking it, in its worktree.

🤖 build worker
Needs-review

PR open + on staging, awaiting review (or the auto-merge gate).

🤖 build worker
Changes-requested

You revised, or a gate failed: back for rework → loops to In-progress.

🧑 /orch revise
Approved → Merged

OK'd + green → lands on main (at kickoff, or auto in run-to-completion).

🧑 or risk-gate
The rework loop is the point

Needs-review doesn't only flow forward. On a revise — or an integration/consistency failure — the epic drops to Changes-requested, a worker picks it up next run, and it comes back to review. It circles until you approve it (gated) or the DoD + risk gate clear it (auto). States are backend-agnostic; signals still come from the forge, never the board.

Step-by-step setup

Provision the board → — a click-by-click guide for Notion, Jira and Linear: the exact menus, the properties and states to create, the token to make (and which kind), and the three commands that prove it works. Twenty minutes, once.

Bring your own board

A Notion, Jira or Linear backend starts with one question at /core:new-project — then /core:board-setup does the rest:

🆕Create from the template

Notion — created for you (MCP connector, no credentials): 12 lifecycle states in order, grouped board view, all properties. Two databases, because the initiative is a real page with its own board; epics and tasks share one source, told apart by a Type select and linked by a Parent epic self-relation (ADR-0030).
Jira — the connector cannot create projects: you create one in the UI (30 seconds), paste its URL, and the skill adapts it.
Linear — nothing to provision: a team already has workflow states and labels, so you name the team and map the 12 lifecycle states onto them. pm-linear files epics as Issues, children as sub-issues, and uses Projects as the initiative tier (ADR-0029) — the closest fit of any backend, since that hierarchy is Linear's own.

📋Adopt an existing board

Paste its URL — Notion database link or Jira project link. Never trusted as-is: it goes through the audit below before anything is recorded.

01

Audit against the contract

The real schema is read and compared: the 12 states in lifecycle order (columns inherit it), plus the required properties — Assigned to (which worker is on the card, cleared on hand-off), Complexity (drives the model choice), Created/Edited timestamps, PR, Note.

02

Gap report

A compact table: what's missing, what has the wrong type, what's out of order. Nothing is touched yet.

03

Your call: fix it, or get the recipe

automatic additive-only — adds what's missing, never deletes, renames or re-types anything already there, and shows a before/after.  yourself a copy-ready guide (exact property names, types, option order, where to click) + an offered re-audit when you're done.

🌱Jira: fresh & dedicated

Native semantics: epics are real Jira Epics, work items are children (parent), state rides real status transitions. You add the 12 columns once in the UI (the API can't — "+" adds, double-click renames, drag reorders); the skill recommends the statusMap and health validates every target.

🏢Jira: existing, with real work

The team's schema is never modified — the 12 lifecycle states map many-to-one onto the statuses that already exist (e.g. Needs-review→Testing). Same Epics/children/transitions, zero workflow surgery.

Degrades safely

The exact state always lives in the epic-record JSON; the Jira status is the human view. An unmapped state, a missing status, or an unreachable transition (workflows are graphs) falls back to orch-state-* labels for that update, logged — a mis-mapped board is a poorer view, never a broken loop (ADR-0021).

What you wake up to

The morning report

Not a log to grep — a single, immutable digest written for a human with coffee. One folder per day (docs/reports/nightly/<date>/ — index.html, summary.md, shots/); a same-day re-run appends a "Run 2" section, never overwrites. Delivered to Slack/email at a time you choose, and persisted to an orch/state branch so a build that finished past midnight still reaches you.

✅Per epic

Summary + PR link + risk class and trust tier (low risk in an auto class = landed; anything else = escalated with the reason), the four DoD gate results, verification screenshots, and the staging route where it's live to click through. The Overview adds run metrics — per-phase token spend measured by the harness itself, never reconstructed from agent logs — and a VCR line (verified ÷ activated; <1 = under-finished work).

🧭Your ten-minute check

The top of the digest is an ordered, human-runnable test sequence: per-epic acceptance checks (action → expected + staging URL), then cross-epic interaction tests wherever footprints overlapped. Pause/resume markers are visible, never silent.

$ caffeinate -s claude -p "/orchestrator:run" --output-format json
  → scope? first 5 epics → [checkout-v2, search, … ] confirm
  → fold prior feedback · plan · build ×N worktrees
  → verify (tests · browser · acceptance · judges) · merge queue
  → morning digest: 3 merged · 1 escalated (auth) · 1 blocked

When it gets something wrong

Three loops that close on the harness itself

A harness that cannot tell you what it got wrong cannot be improved. These are the parts that watch the loop rather than the code.

📓The journal

An append-only .orch/journal/*.jsonl written by hooks, not by the agent: guard blocks, failing commands, human corrections, subagent failures, formatter rewrites, model escalations, reverts. It records a classification, never content — the verb of a failed command, not the command line; the shape of a correction, not your words.

/core:export-journal produces a redacted bundle you can carry back to the marketplace repo. Redaction is an allowlist, so a field added later cannot leak by default, and the exporter verifies its own output and refuses to write if a home path, absolute path, @ or URL survives. No network — it writes a file; moving it is your call.

🎯Standing goals

passes:true used to be terminal: the harness could tell you a feature passed the night it was built and nothing more. Merged epics now graduate their acceptance criteria into shell predicates re-verified daily. A goal you verify once is an assumption with a timestamp.

It detects; it never fixes — a violation goes through the normal pipeline, because an auto-fix on a regression nobody has looked at is how a real bug gets papered over. A predicate that times out counts as a violation, not a skip: treating it as a pass is how a sentinel goes quietly blind.

🔧CI, observed and repaired

The harness used to know a PR was red and never why — nothing read a job log. orch state pull-checks now returns red | pending | green | none plus the failing job's log, and the fix-ci lane triages and repairs the mechanical failures.

Pending is not green — that used to make an unstarted PR read as merge-eligible. Flake, infra and dependency failures escalate rather than being retried until they pass, and the agent cannot edit a workflow file: a guard blocks it.

🌱Compost

Weekly, /orchestrator:compost reads the journal, the trust ledger and the goal ledger and proposes at most three concrete fixes. The question is always the same: is this a rule the harness enforced after the fact that it should have taught up front? A recurring guard block is a missing line in CLAUDE.md; a recurring human correction is a framework problem, not an operator problem.

Three is a ceiling, not a target — a clean week should say so. Proposals only; the guard hooks block a harness from rewriting its own guardrails, which is correct.

the loops policy-lib.sh · journal() journal-export verify-goals.sh fix-ci.js trust (the ledger)
The floor that never moves

Safety model

Two tiers: core guarantees can't be switched off by any profile or mode; the rest apply when the orchestrator runs. Autonomy never trades away a control — it moves the human gate (to scope-at-launch, plan approval, and high-risk), it doesn't remove it.

Autonomy is earned, not configured

Auto-merge needs the risk policy to allow it and the epic's class — <footprint-root>/<complexity> — to have reached tier auto: 20 runs at 95% verified pass. Slow to grant, fast to revoke: the tier is recomputed on every run and a demotion is announced on stderr, which cron mails. A fresh install has no ledger, so nothing auto-merges until a class has a record — the safe default requires no configuration to get.

🔑Secrets stay secret core

Three independent walls (gitignore + deny rules + secret-guard hook), working with variable names, never values. In unattended CI the fail-closed egress firewall is the control — nothing can phone out.

🚫No self-elevation core

It cannot edit the file defining its own permissions, nor the guardrail hooks or allow-listed scripts it runs. It must not rewrite its own referee. One documented Bash-redirection gap stays open deliberately — the real fences are plan-mode, the sandbox, and PR review.

✋Reads before it writes core

Plan-mode by default — it proposes before it writes — and every MCP server is approved one by one.

🧹Git hygiene

Can't skip git safety checks (--no-verify), can't force-push main, can't quietly edit CI files, lockfiles, or accepted ADRs (supersede instead).

🔒Main is gated orchestrator

Gated: nothing reaches main without your per-PR OK + green checks. Run-to-completion: low-risk work in a class that has earned tier auto lands after DoD + judges + the CODEOWNERS double gate; everything else escalates. Workers only push throwaway orch/* branches.

🧪Risky changes: a second gate orchestrator

Big diffs or anything touching auth / payments / migrations / infra are auto-flagged, need a security-auditor pass to be merge-eligible, and CODEOWNERS forces a human review at the forge — risk gated twice, independently.

📦Unattended runs are boxed in orchestrator

Four walls: deny rules → fail-closed guard hooks (they block if jq is missing) → native OS sandbox (egress allowlist + credentials denied to subprocesses, MCP pinned to playwright) → the devcontainer's default-deny firewall — the last two fed by ONE allowlist, parity-tested. Committed settings never touched.

🛑Escalation is the default

Unknown risk classifies high (fail closed); a crashed consistency checker keeps the deploy gate shut; a red post-merge suite auto-reverts.

// orchestrator/risk-policy.json — data the operator owns; re-read every run
{ "linesChanged": { "low": 150, "medium": 600 },        // > medium ⇒ high
  "highRiskPaths": ["**/auth/**","**/payment/**","**/migrations/**","**/infra/**",".github/workflows/**"],
  "autoMergeRiskLevels": ["low"],                        // only these merge unattended
  "requiredReviewByRisk": { "low":"judge-panel", "high":"human-codeowners" } }
enforced by secret-guard.sh protect-paths.sh block-no-verify.sh protect-policy-paths.sh hooks.json (wiring) risk-policy.json CODEOWNERS settings.orchestrator.json egress-allowlist.txt (one source, two walls) verdict.schema.json test-codeowners-risk-parity.sh
The specialists

Agents — who does what

The loop delegates to focused subagents, each with a restricted toolset and a model matched to the job. The load-bearing ones for autonomy: design-reviewer (gates plans and DoDs), security-auditor (the second gate on risky merges), integration-checker (verifies merged overlapping epics still work together), ci-triage (reads a failing job's log and classifies it — diagnoses, never edits).

AgentPluginModelFires when
code-reviewercoresonnetProactively after any significant change — correctness, conventions, simplicity. Reports, never edits.
debuggercoreinheritA bug resists first diagnosis — reproduce / isolate / root-cause with evidence.
architectcoreopusA structural decision → options + an ADR draft. Never contradicts an accepted ADR silently.
design-reviewercoreopusBefore freezing a spec/plan/DoD — adversarial critique; READY / READY-WITH-FIXES / NEEDS-REWORK.
docs-writercorehaikuDoc layer drift — CODEMAP, STACK, CHANGELOG, ROADMAP consistency.
plannerorchestratoropusDecomposes initiatives into epics + authors each DoD and a complexity estimate (drives model choice). Never writes product code, never self-approves.
integration-checkerorchestratorsonnetOverlapping epics merged → verifies the combined result still meets each epic's criteria.
ci-triageorchestratorsonnetA PR goes red → reads the failing job's log, reproduces locally, classifies (regression / type / lint / flake / infra / dependency) and proposes the smallest fix. Diagnoses; never edits. Flake, infra and dependency escalate rather than being "fixed".
security-auditorworkbenchopusBefore sensitive merges — OWASP, secrets, personal data; required for high-risk PRs.
refactorerworkbenchsonnetMass mechanical change in an isolated worktree.
researcherworkbenchsonnetExternal knowledge with sources, in the background.
test-runnerworkbenchsonnetRuns the suite, analyzes failures; never fixes.
Rules of thumb

Parallel only if files are disjoint — read-only agents parallelize safely; writers get worktrees. Vague invocation is failure mode #1 — exact paths + a success criterion, always. Below ~3 independent subtasks, coordination costs more than it gains.

Memory

The state layer

Sessions, specs, epics, plans and status all go through one CLI contract with a pluggable backend — plain sharded files in the repo (none, zero-setup) or your real board (GitHub Projects / GitLab / Jira / Linear / Notion / Trello adapters).

# the contract — same ops on every backend
orch state health                         # backend reachable / auth OK
orch state push-session < session.json    # end-of-session snapshot
orch state pull-session                   # startup injection reads here
orch state push-epic · push-status        # one file per epic — no shared table
orch state pull-status                    # aggregated AT READ TIME
orch state pull-feedback                  # ALWAYS from the forge (gh/glab)
orch state push-digest --date D < d.html  # the daily report
orch state pull-checks [--pr N]           # CI: red|pending|green|none + failing job logs
orch state list-initiatives               # the tier, native or derived per backend
orch state claim --id E [--ttl MIN]       # lease a card; expires so a crash can't strand it
orch state push-journal · pull-journal    # the harness's own error/correction log (local only)

🧩Sharded, not shared

One small file per branch/epic — two parallel workers never write the same file, and git merges them with zero conflicts (property-tested). Status aggregates at read time.

✉️State ≠ feedback

Tasks can live anywhere, but approvals are always read from the code host, never the board. Signals only count from trusted authors (owner/member/collaborator).

🏛️The board outlives the loop

Chosen once at scaffold, reused when you enable autonomy, left fully intact when you disable it.

🛟Fail-open injection

At session start it reads local → remote (with a timeout) → cache — a slow board never stalls a session; a corrupt state file is skipped loudly, never blanks the board.

📓One append-only stream

Everything else here is replace-semantics. .orch/journal/*.jsonl is the only history: guard blocks, failing commands, human corrections, escalations, reverts — written by hooks, so it does not depend on the agent choosing to be honest. It records classifications, never content.

📈Two ledgers

trust.tsv — has this class of work earned the right to land unattended. goal-ledger.tsv — is everything we already finished still true. Read both with coffee.

the layer orch (the CLI) state.config.json adapters/ (5 implemented + 1 stub) inject-session.sh test-orch-state.sh (zero-conflict property)

Provenance

Tests & verified deviations

Every subsystem shipped test-first, in this order — each green before the next: ① the DoD contract + independent verifier, ② the planner, ③ the driver + concurrency + guards, ④ risk-gated auto-merge + safety wiring, ⑤ packaging + docs. Before building, each design was checked against the July 2026 state of the art; the deltas live in docs/DEVIATIONS.md — including a full audit against the learn-harness-engineering lectures 04–13 (§7: five practices adopted — day-0 harness, verifier-owned evidence, per-phase metrics + VCR, clean-exit checklist, instruction audit — and three rejected with reasons). An external market audit (v1.4.x round) hardened the plugin further — fail-closed guards, hook timeouts, CI on the marketplace itself, keychain-backed config, deterministic packaging. A market-baseline audit scored every dimension with evidence — enforcement, verification, context hygiene and security landed ABOVE; the one deliberate BELOW is cross-tool interop: this harness is Claude Code native by design (ADR-0022 — the edge is the enforcement layer, which only Claude Code runs).

⚖️Judge panel, decorrelated

Same-model majority votes ≈ one judge (correlated-errors research), so each lens pins a distinct model; ties and zero votes always fail.

🔐Risk fails closed

Risk is computed from the real git diff; a missing policy, unknown branch, or unreadable diff classifies high — nothing merges on a shrug. (Fixes a reference-implementation gap where the loop hardcoded low.)

🎫Auth lanes, verified

Subscription lane first: claude setup-token → CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (~1 year), never combined with --bare (which skips OAuth). ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is the metered lane and takes precedence — leave it unset otherwise. On the local runtime there is no token at all: the loop uses the CLI you are already logged into, so nothing long-lived sits in a secret store (ADR-0033).

🏖️Native sandbox on top

Claude Code's OS sandbox (write-scoping, credential deny, network allowlist) is enabled in the unattended profile, in addition to the devcontainer's egress firewall.

If you build one thing first

Build the definition-of-done contract and its independent verifier before the fancy driver. The loop is easy; a trustworthy "done" is the hard, valuable part. Once an epic can be proven finished by something other than its author, everything else — concurrency, auto-merge, scheduling — is plumbing you add incrementally, gate by gate.
